_help: Track B: Secondary citation. Items are grouped by stage. See README.md, section 'How to add or edit an item'.
title: Secondary citation

items.prompt: You read a 2021 textbook by Osei. In Chapter 3, Osei describes a 2014 study by Varga on study habits. You did not read Varga's study. Which is true?
options: Original: Varga (2014). Source I read: Osei (2021).
Original: Osei (2021). Source I read: Varga (2014).
I read both Varga (2014) and Osei (2021).
acceptedAnswers: Original: Varga (2014). Source I read: Osei (2021).
items.rule: Secondary, in brackets: (Original, year, as cited in Source you read, year).
items.hint: The original idea is the older study. You held only one book in your hands.

items.prompt: In their 2019 book, Tanaka and Brennan summarise a 2008 survey by Alvarez. You read only the book. Which is true?
options: Original: Alvarez (2008). Source I read: Tanaka and Brennan (2019).
Original: Tanaka and Brennan (2019). Source I read: Alvarez (2008).
Original: Tanaka (2019). Source I read: Brennan (2019).
acceptedAnswers: Original: Alvarez (2008). Source I read: Tanaka and Brennan (2019).
items.rule: Secondary, in brackets: (Original, year, as cited in Source you read, year).
items.hint: Who did the survey? Whose book did you read?

items.prompt: You found Kowalski's 2012 article mentioned in a 2020 article by Moretti. Then you found Kowalski's article in the library and read it. Which is true?
options: I read Kowalski (2012) myself, so I cite Kowalski directly.
I must write (Kowalski, 2012, as cited in Moretti, 2020).
I cite only Moretti (2020), because that is where I found the idea.
acceptedAnswers: I read Kowalski (2012) myself, so I cite Kowalski directly.
items.rule: Use “as cited in” only when you cannot get the original. Reading the original is better.
items.hint: You read the original yourself in the end.

items.prompt: You read a 2022 book by Halvorsen. Halvorsen quotes a saying by Mwangi, but does not give a year for it. Which is true?
options: Original: Mwangi (year unknown). Source I read: Halvorsen (2022).
Original: Halvorsen (2022). Source I read: Mwangi (year unknown).
There is no original, so I cite only Halvorsen (2022).
acceptedAnswers: Original: Mwangi (year unknown). Source I read: Halvorsen (2022).
items.rule: Secondary, in brackets: (Original, year, as cited in Source you read, year). If the original year is unknown, leave it out.
items.hint: There is no year for the original, but you still know who said it.

items.prompt: You read a 2023 web article by Kaur. Kaur reports what Delgado found in a 2016 study. You did not read Delgado's study. Which is true?
options: Original: Delgado (2016). Source I read: Kaur (2023).
Original: Kaur (2023). Source I read: Delgado (2016).
I read both Delgado (2016) and Kaur (2023).
acceptedAnswers: Original: Delgado (2016). Source I read: Kaur (2023).
items.rule: Secondary, in brackets: (Original, year, as cited in Source you read, year).
items.hint: Who found the results? Whose article was on your screen?

items.prompt: You read Nasser's 2018 article. Nasser quotes a sentence from Iyer's 2001 book. You did not read Iyer's book. Which is true?
options: Original: Iyer (2001). Source I read: Nasser (2018).
Original: Nasser (2018). Source I read: Iyer (2001).
Original: Nasser (2018). Source I read: Nasser (2018).
acceptedAnswers: Original: Iyer (2001). Source I read: Nasser (2018).
items.rule: Secondary, in brackets: (Original, year, as cited in Source you read, year).
items.hint: Whose words are they? Whose article did you read?

items.prompt: You read a 2019 report by the National Centre for Urban Transport. The report describes a 2011 survey by Petrova about bus use. You did not read Petrova's survey. Which is true?
options: Original: Petrova (2011). Source I read: National Centre for Urban Transport (2019).
Original: National Centre for Urban Transport (2019). Source I read: Petrova (2011).
I read both Petrova (2011) and the report (2019).
acceptedAnswers: Original: Petrova (2011). Source I read: National Centre for Urban Transport (2019).
items.rule: Secondary, in brackets: (Original, year, as cited in Source you read, year).
items.hint: Who did the survey? Which report did you read?

items.prompt: In their 2020 article, Sandoval and Kariuki summarise Romano's 2009 book on reading habits. You read only the article. Which is true?
options: Original: Romano (2009). Source I read: Sandoval and Kariuki (2020).
Original: Sandoval and Kariuki (2020). Source I read: Romano (2009).
Original: Sandoval (2020). Source I read: Kariuki (2020).
acceptedAnswers: Original: Romano (2009). Source I read: Sandoval and Kariuki (2020).
items.rule: Secondary, in brackets: (Original, year, as cited in Source you read, year).
items.hint: Whose book is the idea from? Whose article did you read?

items.prompt: You read a 2017 article by Castillo. Castillo mentions an older study by Okafor, but you use only Castillo's own ideas in your essay. Which is true?
options: I cite Castillo (2017) directly. I do not need to mention Okafor.
I must cite (Okafor, as cited in Castillo, 2017).
I must cite both Okafor and Castillo.
acceptedAnswers: I cite Castillo (2017) directly. I do not need to mention Okafor.
items.rule: Cite the person whose idea you use. If you use only Castillo's ideas, cite Castillo directly.
items.hint: Whose ideas are you actually using?

items.prompt: You read a 2024 web article by Brennan. Brennan reports what Tanaka found in a 2015 experiment. You did not read Tanaka's report. Which is true?
options: Original: Tanaka (2015). Source I read: Brennan (2024).
Original: Brennan (2024). Source I read: Tanaka (2015).
I read both Tanaka (2015) and Brennan (2024).
acceptedAnswers: Original: Tanaka (2015). Source I read: Brennan (2024).
items.rule: Secondary, in brackets: (Original, year, as cited in Source you read, year).
items.hint: Who did the experiment? Whose article was on your screen?

items.prompt: Why does only the source you read go in the reference list?
options: It tells readers exactly which sources you used, so they can find them.
Older sources are less important, so they are left out.
APA does not allow two references for one idea.
acceptedAnswers: It tells readers exactly which sources you used, so they can find them.
items.rule: Only the source you actually read goes in the reference list.
items.hint: Think about what a reader does with your reference list.

items.prompt: Your textbook (Osei, 2021) describes Varga's 2014 study. The library has Varga's article online, and you can read it. What should you do?
options: Read Varga's article and cite Varga directly.
Use “as cited in”, because it is quicker.
Cite only Osei, as if the idea were Osei's.
acceptedAnswers: Read Varga's article and cite Varga directly.
items.rule: Use “as cited in” only when you cannot get the original. Reading the original is better.
items.hint: Is the original available to you?

items.prompt: Osei (2021) describes a 1985 report by Brennan. The report was never published online, and no library you can use has it. What should you do?
options: Use a secondary citation: (Brennan, 1985, as cited in Osei, 2021).
Cite Brennan (1985) directly, as if you had read it.
Cite only Osei (2021) and do not mention Brennan.
acceptedAnswers: Use a secondary citation: (Brennan, 1985, as cited in Osei, 2021).
items.rule: Use “as cited in” only when you cannot get the original. Reading the original is better.
items.hint: Can you get the original?

items.prompt: You read Moretti's original article yourself. You want to use one of Moretti's findings. What should you do?
options: Cite Moretti directly, e.g. (Moretti, 2020).
Use “as cited in” to be safe.
Do not cite it, because findings are facts.
acceptedAnswers: Cite Moretti directly, e.g. (Moretti, 2020).
items.rule: If you read the original, cite it directly. No “as cited in” is needed.
items.hint: Did you read the original?

items.prompt: You read only a short summary of Delgado's study in Kaur et al. (2023). You want to use Delgado's results in your essay. What should you do?
options: Find and read Delgado's study. If you cannot get it, use “as cited in Kaur et al., 2023”.
Cite (Delgado, 2016) directly. The summary is enough.
Cite (Delgado, 2016; Kaur et al., 2023).
acceptedAnswers: Find and read Delgado's study. If you cannot get it, use “as cited in Kaur et al., 2023”.
items.rule: Use “as cited in” only when you cannot get the original. Reading the original is better. Citing a source you did not read as if you read it is an integrity problem.
items.hint: Did you read Delgado's study, or only a summary of it?

items.prompt: Osei (2021) describes Varga's study, then gives Osei's own opinion about it. You want to use Osei's opinion, not Varga's results. What should you do?
options: Cite Osei (2021) only.
Use (Varga, 2014, as cited in Osei, 2021).
Cite Varga (2014) only.
acceptedAnswers: Cite Osei (2021) only.
items.rule: Cite the person whose idea you use. Osei's own opinion is cited to Osei.
items.hint: Whose idea are you using?

items.prompt: Osei (2021) summarises a study by Yilmaz that was published only in Turkish. You cannot read Turkish. What should you do?
options: Use a secondary citation: Yilmaz (2010, as cited in Osei, 2021).
Cite Yilmaz (2010) directly, as if you had read it.
Leave the idea out completely, because you cannot cite it.
acceptedAnswers: Use a secondary citation: Yilmaz (2010, as cited in Osei, 2021).
items.rule: Use “as cited in” only when you cannot get the original. Reading the original is better.
items.hint: Can you read the original?
